“In the ’20s, imagine what that was like. That was the first time you had electricity in houses, so you had lighting and you had refrigeration. posts.text:
Cyberpunk 2077 is starting to look less like science fiction and more like an extreme extrapolation of modern America.

The central premise of cyberpunk is "high tech, low life": extraordinary technological advancement without a corresponding improvement in everyone's quality of life.

Consider the parallels:

- Arasaka and Militech: Technology and defense giants becoming increasingly intertwined with government and national security.

- Corporate political power: Billionaires increasingly influencing elections, government policy and regulation.

- Corporate surveillance: AI-powered monitoring, facial recognition and commercial data brokers.

- Trauma Team: A healthcare system where access and quality are heavily influenced by personal wealth.*

- Cybernetic augmentation: Neuralink, brain-computer interfaces and advanced prosthetics.

- Rogue AI and the Blackwall: Autonomous AI agents, cybersecurity threats and increasingly powerful artificial intelligence.

- Corporate-controlled infrastructure: Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Nvidia and SpaceX controlling critical technological infrastructure.

- Extreme class divisions: Concentrated asset ownership, deteriorating housing affordability and enormous disparities in wealth.

- Digital escapism: AI companions, immersive virtual worlds and algorithmically addictive entertainment.

America is obviously nowhere near Night City in terms of violence, institutional collapse or corporate sovereignty. Democratic institutions and legal protections still constrain corporate power.

But the underlying trajectory is remarkably similar: technological abundance alongside economic insecurity, increasingly powerful corporations alongside governments dependent on their capabilities, and extraordinary private wealth alongside persistent social problems.

Perhaps the most interesting thing about Cyberpunk 2077 is that it depicts a future in which capitalism and technological innovation succeed spectacularly, but society fails to distribute their benefits broadly.

Technological progress does not automatically translate into social progress.

*The trauma team intro is the best part of the game?

October 28 results independently showed organic orders increasing more than 100% and organic revenue increasing 55%. HPE therefore provides customer-side corroboration of the infrastructure bottleneck, not the first evidence of the cycle. This distinction reduces the justification for treating the call as a standalone near-term earnings upgrade.

The timing implication is more nuanced than simply moving every supplier forecast into HPE’s second half. Some power and cooling equipment must be delivered before IT systems are installed; commissioning can occur later. HPE’s schedule confirms dependency on facility completion but does not establish Vertiv’s project-specific order or revenue dates.

Near-term catalyst: Backlog conversion, installation progress, commissioning, and customer site-readiness disclosures are more actionable than aggregate AI-order announcements. Delayed facilities can defer IT revenue even when underlying demand remains intact.

Longer-duration implication: Rising rack density and more complex liquid-cooled infrastructure support higher engineering and service requirements. However, liquid cooling transfers heat rather than eliminating it, and specific chiller, heat-exchanger, or fluid-distribution content depends on architecture. The high-conviction read-through is sustained demand for critical infrastructure, not an undisclosed HPE design win or a universal increase in every cooling component.

I like this and I can get behind most of it. Regime risk is real and trend is one of the best tools for it, which is why I own it. 

Where I get stuck is the core part (or sizing the asset match right, as it pertains to my framework). The T-bill collateral is great, but I can own T-bills directly, and in an ALM framework that's exactly what funds the near-term liabilities. The overlay on top is what I'm evaluating, and it has no cash flows I can use to estimate a return or match against a liability. Structurally agnostic to direction isn't the same as unconditional either. It still needs sustained trends. 

And on the sequence math, the research points to the first decade of real returns, not the first five years. That's where trend's lost-decade risk shows up. So, in an ALM framework this isn't really a debate about whether to use trend, but whether trend is a better long-term matching instrument than other long-term options (clearly better than long duration bonds, but that argument is not nearly as robust compared to equities). The long-term stuff is, as @choffstein says, a statistical bet and there's no clear winner there given past isn't indicative of future returns and all that....

So I'd frame it this way: the core is whatever I can plan around, and trend is insurance against the core's assumptions breaking. That case gets me to a bigger satellite, maybe 15%+. It doesn't get me to a foundation on its own (which is where a multi-asset "stacked" instrument probably makes a more appealing core argument). 

Again, none of this is an argument against trend (definitely not against stacking trend). It's a quibble over trend as the main asset in a portfolio when compared to something like equities where, as I recently framed it in my 50 page research piece (which, no one read as well, lol), I framed the opportunity cost as potentially gigantic in the long-run. But as you note, that's basically a bet on stable Capitalism in the future, and  I feel pretty good about that bet.

I’m usually a fan of the @davidmcw podcast, but episodes 93 and 95 on Jensen Huang and AI contained some significant inaccuracies. Three examples:

Neoclouds: The suggestion that neoclouds rent capacity from hyperscalers gets the business model backwards.
They finance and operate GPU infrastructure, then rent compute to AI companies and other customers including Microsoft.

Open models: The discussion of Jensen’s position on China and AI overlooks his strong advocacy for open models. This is central to understanding his position.

Who captures the profits? The claim that Taiwan and Korea manufacture the chips and pocket the real profits overlooks Nvidia’s economics. CUDA, GPU architecture, networking and integrated systems give Nvidia enormous pricing power and margins. It is far more than a chip designer outsourcing manufacturing.

These aren't minor technical details. They fundamentally shape how listeners understand the AI industry. You can be sceptical about AI valuations without getting the underlying economics wrong.

In a wild turn of events, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia yesterday. The news will be regurgitated in every media outlet around the world, so I am only going to focus on my takeaways this morning.

First, Jensen just solidified his spot on the Mount Rushmore of technology founders. No one else could return to the company they founded three decades ago and watch the US stock market increase by $3 trillion in a matter of minutes. It was surreal watching the market surge in real-time as the news spread, but maybe we shouldn’t be surprised given Jensen is largely thought of as the godfather of the AI industry.

Second, this is a great reminder that the voice of shareholders will usually be heard. The board of directors misplayed their hand and tried to over-govern the situation. Given the immediate and severe sell-off in Nvidia’s stock price, it is clear that shareholders disagreed with the board’s decision to force Jensen to resign. Add in the ridiculous stock recovery of more than 30% upon his return and it is clear that shareholders want Jensen at the helm of the company.

Third, Jensen needs to immediately remove the entire board of directors. He can’t operate a business with board members that were willing to force him out of his company and risk trillions of dollars in shareholder value. These directors showed their true colors, which is now a risk to Nvidia. For better or worse, you need directors that are loyal to the company and shareholders, not a group of people whose opinion will blow with the wind of public sentiment.

Fourth, the AI trade is about to catch a second wind. The recent market sell-off gave everyone time to take a deep breath, but demand is still outstripping supply, so we are going much higher.

CROSS-PORTFOLIO RISK: MORE AI SUPPLIERS DO NOT NECESSARILY PROVIDE MORE DIVERSIFICATION (READ-THROUGH 11)

Affected companies: Analog Devices (ADI: US), Monolithic Power Systems (MPWR: US), Teradyne (TER: US), Coherent (COHR: US), Lumentum Holdings (LITE: US), and Vertiv Holdings (VRT: US). Direction: negative for diversification assumptions, despite the positive operating outlook. Magnitude: potentially high for portfolios holding several of these exposures.

ADI’s direct data-center revenue represented approximately 13% of sales, but management grouped data center, ATE, and aerospace and defense into a larger approximately 30% revenue pool benefiting from unusually strong demand. Additional AI-linked demand appears in energy, power infrastructure, and automation. Consequently, direct data-center reporting understates some companies’ economic sensitivity to the infrastructure investment cycle.

The transmission mechanism is a shared final spending driver across different supply-chain stages. Hyperscaler and accelerator-platform investment supports optical connectivity, power semiconductors, semiconductor test, and cooling infrastructure. These businesses have different products, customers, and shipment timing, but a change in deployment schedules or infrastructure budgets can propagate through several holdings simultaneously.

ADI’s statement that more than 2/3 of fiscal 2026 growth came from non-AI-centric opportunities remains an important offset. ADI is not a pure-play AI supplier, and the affected companies should not be treated as having identical sensitivities. Nevertheless, product diversification and numerous SKUs do not establish independence from the same ultimate capital-spending decisions.

The near-term risk is correlated trading during semiconductor and AI-infrastructure de-risking, even when individual earnings releases remain strong. The longer-duration risk is that supply-chain orders, inventory buffers, and capacity expansions amplify a subsequent change in final demand. The portfolio implication is to aggregate these exposures by underlying infrastructure spending and cash-flow dependence, rather than treating analog chips, optical components, test equipment, and cooling systems as fully separate risk categories.

posts.name: James Seyffart
posts.text:
There's tons of pros and cons to defined benefit vs defined contribution. I personally think its not all that close. I would (and do) prefer defined contribution if i were given the option.

1. as max and you already said. job mobility and portability of these plans doesn't work as its set up. Its simply not in line with the current way the job market works. 

2. Its fairly common for pensions to not include CLOA's for inflation etc. A fixed pension giving you $50k per year in 2000 is at least half as valuable as it was then.

3.  there's funding sponsor risk. There are back stops from ERISA and other things but if the company goes bankrupt that's a real potential problem and would likely lead to less money for many people in that pension plan. For public pensions its not as worrisome because they'll just increase taxes on citizens to fund it (or cut benefits from the pensioners to better balance the books)

4. Way way wayyy less flexibility. Cant change withdrawal rate. Cant change your investments to dial up or down the risk. You basically get a fixed annuity (which isn't neccessarily bad)

5. If you want that fixed annuity you can use your retirement funds in defined contribution world to buy exactly that! 

If you are going to spend the bulk of your adult life working for a stable and successful employer that will never go out of business and offers you a pension with CLOAs... that is an *excellent* retirement solution. Basically 10 out of 10. but that's a lot of "ifs" and it doesn't automatically make them the best retirement saving system for everyone or even a flexible workforce where the average person changes their job every ~5 years.

Not to mention the fact that most pensions are underfunded in the US -- much like social security.

posts.text:
From The Dotcom Bust To The AI Boom History Warns Of A Growing Credit Risk

The hyperscaler credit default swap basket reached 115.6 on November 24, rising approximately 12% from its November lows and reaching a new high within the displayed period.

This is particularly concerning because skepticism surrounding AI is increasingly spreading beyond equity valuations into corporate credit markets, where investors are reassessing financial sustainability and demanding greater compensation for credit risk.

Yesterday’s extraordinary equity rally following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement restored some investor confidence. It did not resolve the underlying financing vulnerabilities.

Historical Precedent

During the telecommunications boom of the late 1990s, companies committed enormous amounts of capital toward infrastructure based on expectations of explosive future internet demand.

Technology credit spreads began widening in early 2000 before the broader investment cycle collapsed. Financing became increasingly restrictive, capital expenditure contracted and bankruptcies followed.

The internet ultimately revolutionized the global economy. That did not prevent enormous financial losses among the institutions financing its initial expansion.

Similarly, during 2007, financial sector credit spreads began deteriorating before the full extent of the economic contraction became apparent.

Today, AI may represent another transformative technological advancement accompanied by an unsustainable investment cycle.

The Growing Financing Problem

Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr recently identified several vulnerabilities within the AI financing ecosystem.

•  More than $800 billion in projected corporate debt among seven major AI companies by year end

•  More than $3 trillion in potential contractual and other financial obligations

•  More than $100 billion in cumulative equity investments by hyperscalers and GPU producers in AI laboratories and cloud startups

These exposures are not equivalent to outstanding debt and should not be added together. Nevertheless, they reveal considerable financial interconnectedness.

Companies are increasingly financing customers that purchase their infrastructure, creating demand that may depend heavily on continued access to external capital rather than independently generated revenue.

Meanwhile, long duration debt is financing equipment that faces rapid technological depreciation and potential obsolescence.

The Macroeconomic Transmission

AI investment has become an important source of economic growth, supporting semiconductor manufacturing, construction, electrical infrastructure, utilities, logistics and professional services.

These industries appear independently throughout economic statistics, yet portions of their demand originate from the same investment cycle.

Persistent credit spread widening could increase borrowing costs, undermine investment returns, delay infrastructure projects and eventually force capital expenditure reductions and workforce restructuring.

This is developing while household delinquency is rising, small business bankruptcies are accelerating, commercial real estate remains distressed and labor market hiring is historically subdued.

Unlike previous investment busts, persistent energy inflation is also limiting the Federal Reserve’s ability to provide monetary relief.

The greatest concern is that financial market deleveraging is beginning to threaten one of the principal investment cycles sustaining aggregate economic growth.

Widening hyperscaler CDS spreads do not establish an imminent credit crisis. However, historical precedent demonstrates why the transition from deteriorating equity valuations to deteriorating credit conditions deserves considerably greater attention.

The equity market can celebrate technological potential. The credit market must ultimately determine whether the financial obligations incurred to realize that potential can be serviced.

JUST IN: Attorney General Todd Blanche says the national-security call on Jensen Huang was a collective consensus across agencies, and that he has no information on Huang's clearance status

Q: "How did the administration, though, just setting aside the potential criminal investigations, actually make a determination that there was no national security risk related to Jensen Huang? And who, is it DOJ, is it the Pentagon, is assessing Huang's continuing access to sensitive national security information?"

BLANCHE: "How we make that type of determination is, there's a whole bunch of ways we do it. We use the intelligence community, the FBI, the information we know. We talk to witnesses. I mean, that's something that we do."

"I know there's heightened focus on this situation, but that's something that the law enforcement partners and that the leadership in this country, whether it's commerce or treasury, state department, the attorney general, me, it's a collective consensus that we reach all the time in all kinds of different cases, not just in this case."

"And how we determine whether a private citizen has access to information, I mean, there's clearances, there's background clearances, there's information that, depending on the project or the job, they're allowed to have or not allowed to have. So it depends on the issue specifically."

"I don't have any information about even what his clearance status is. But I don't know. I mean, I don't want you to take that as an indication that he is or is not keeping his clearance. I just have no information about that."
